label: Memory is defined functionally as future behaviour modulated by past experience
claim: In the basal cognition framework adopted by Biswas, Clawson and Levin, memory is defined in substrate-independent functionalist terms: a system has memory when its future behaviour is specifically modulated by its past experience, which allows the question of whether molecular networks such as gene regulatory networks are trainable.
quote: Consistent with the basal cognition paradigm, we define memory in functionalist terms—a system in which future behavior is specifically modulated by past experience.
scope: Any system, including gene regulatory networks and protein pathways
candidate_data: none known

label: Published ODE models of gene and protein pathways show several kinds of memory
claim: In simulations of 35 published ODE models of gene regulatory networks and protein/metabolic pathways from BioModels, the networks show several distinct kinds of memory (UCS-based, pairing, transfer, associative and consolidation memory) in response to patterns of node stimulation.
quote: Here, we characterize biological gene regulatory circuit models and protein pathways and find them capable of several different kinds of memory.
scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels (bacteria, slime mould, yeast, plants, vertebrates, mammals)
measurable_quantities: fraction of stimulus-response node triplets showing each memory type
persistence of response-node expression after stimulus removal
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models; time-course expression data in the Gene Expression Omnibus for the modelled pathways.

label: Nearly all surveyed pathway models have memory; very small networks may not
claim: Memory was found in all but four of the 35 surveyed BioModels pathway models, and three of those four had fewer than four nodes, suggesting that very small networks either cannot have, or are very unlikely to have, memory.
quote: Overall, we found memory models in all surveyed biological networks except four models, of which three had a low number of nodes (<4) suggesting that too small networks either cannot, or are very unlikely to, have memory
scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels
measurable_quantities: network size (nodes)
presence of any memory type per model
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: No simple network-topology measure predicts memory in pathway models
claim: Across the 35 surveyed BioModels pathway models, the amount of memory showed no significant correlation with mean number of nodes, edges, degree or hubness, so no single network property is indicative of memory.
quote: Additionally, we tested to see if certain network properties, such as mean number of nodes, edges, degree, and hubness were associated with more or less memory and found there were no significant correlations with any of these measures and any memory (see Discussion).
scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels
measurable_quantities: node count
edge count
degree
hubness
memory capacity per model
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Pathway memories can form through dynamics alone, without structural change
claim: In ODE models of biological pathways, memories (such as associative memory, in which a neutral stimulus becomes a conditioned stimulus) can be formed by patterns of stimulation through dynamical interactions alone, without changing the network's structure or parameters.
quote: Again, while feedback loop architecture is present, our results indicate that memories can be formed through dynamical interactions alone, without changing network structure/architecture.
scope: ODE models of gene regulatory and protein pathways (e.g. MAPK cascade models)
measurable_quantities: response-node expression before and after paired stimulation
network parameters held constant
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models; time-course expression data from pulsed-stimulation experiments in the Gene Expression Omnibus.

label: Feedback loops may be conducive to pathway memory but are not the only route
claim: Self-sustaining feedback loops with hysteresis, such as the positive-feedback dual phosphorylation–dephosphorylation cycle of MAPK, may be conducive to memory in biochemical networks, but feedback loop architecture may be only one of many ways to support such memories.
quote: Overall, we suggest that feedback loop network architecture may be conducive to memories but may be only one way of many to support them.
scope: Biochemical reaction networks, e.g. MAPK phosphorylation cycles
measurable_quantities: presence of positive feedback loops
hysteresis in dose-response
memory capacity
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models; published MAPK hysteresis measurements.

label: Pathway-model memories are robust to a wide range of stimulus strengths
claim: In the surveyed ODE pathway models, memory formation is robust to training stimuli of 10x, 50x and 100x baseline (most models kept the same number of memories and only 10% lost memories), and some models formed more memories with weaker stimulation.
quote: We conclude that the memory properties are robust to a wide range of stimulus strengths, a desirable property for therapeutics, and also for functional linkages with other cell pathways during evolution.
scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels
measurable_quantities: number of memories per model at different stimulus amplitudes
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Noise increases memory in pathway models, especially associative memory
claim: Adding stochastic noise to simulations of the surveyed ODE pathway models left memories intact in most models (83%) and increased memory overall by about 20%, most notably associative memory, suggesting that biological noise does not inhibit and may help the trainability of such networks.
quote: Interestingly, while almost all models retained the memories created (83%), there was an overall 20% increase in memory in the presence of noise (averaged across models and memory phenotypes) most notably in the associative memory paradigm.
scope: 35 ODE pathway models from BioModels with added stochasticity
measurable_quantities: memory capacity with and without noise
noise amplitude
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Most pathway-model memories persist over long periods and survive recall
claim: In the surveyed ODE pathway models with UCS-based memory, most networks retain the bulk of their memories over waiting periods up to 100 times the initial one, and testing (recalling) a memory generally does not destroy it and in rare cases strengthens it.
quote: Overall, we conclude that while some networks have a limit on how long they retain training, the majority of networks can retain the bulk of their possible memories over very long time periods and that in general, memory ‘access’ does not destroy the memory but can, in some rare cases, increase memory.
scope: 30 ODE pathway models from BioModels showing UCS-based memory
measurable_quantities: fraction of memories retained after 10x and 100x delays
change in memory after repeated testing
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Serially trained associative memories cause catastrophic forgetting in pathway models
claim: When two associative memories are trained one after another in ODE pathway models, all biological and random models show catastrophic forgetting in which both memories are lost, whereas two UCS-based memories can be stored serially or in parallel.
quote: When more complex memories were tested, here AM-AM memory pairs, when created serially all biological and random models showed catastrophic forgetting wherein both are lost.
scope: 35 BioModels pathway models and 35 size-matched random gene-circuit models
measurable_quantities: fraction of node assignments retaining both, one or neither memory after serial or parallel training
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Pathway memory is distributed uniformly across organism classes
claim: Memory in the surveyed pathway models shows no privileged association with any class of organism (bacteria, slime mould, yeast, plants, lower vertebrates, mammals), being distributed roughly uniformly, which may suggest that proto-cognitive capacity is found across many strata of life.
quote: We found no privileged categorization of memory over classes of organisms—memory seemed distributed uniformly over all strata of life (see Figure S3).
scope: 35 BioModels pathway models grouped by source organism
measurable_quantities: memory capacity per model grouped by taxon
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models with organism annotations.

label: Biological pathway models have more memory than structurally matched random networks
claim: Compared with 500 random gene-circuit networks matched to the biological models in size, edges, degree, betweenness, PageRank and hubness, the biological ODE pathway models show higher prevalence of most memory types, fewer no-memory cases, and more correlated memory types, indicating that generic network dynamics are not solely responsible for trainability.
quote: Random networks do not show similar memory behavior as models of biological processes, indicating that generic network dynamics are not solely responsible for trainability.
scope: 35 BioModels pathway models versus 500 random synthetic gene-circuit ODE models
measurable_quantities: average prevalence of each memory type
correlation matrix of memory types
fraction of no-memory triplets
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Standard topology measures are likely insufficient to design or evolve memory
claim: Because random networks matched to biological pathway models in number of nodes, edges, indegree, outdegree, betweenness, PageRank and hubness lack comparable memory, those structural features are not likely to be sufficient criteria for designing or evolving networks with memories.
quote: Interestingly, since the random networks were designed to match the biological models in number of nodes, number of edges, indegree, outdegree, betweenness, PageRank, and hubness, those features are not likely to be sufficient criteria for designing (or evolving) networks with memories.
scope: Gene regulatory and protein pathway networks
measurable_quantities: network topology measures
memory capacity
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Pathway memory is more robust to edge perturbation, perhaps from selection
claim: The memory capacity of biological ODE pathway models degrades significantly less than that of random networks when edges are randomly deleted and added, perhaps because of evolutionary pressure to handle changing environments.
quote: The memory capability of biological models is also much more robust to edge perturbation than those of random networks, as indicated in Figure 7, perhaps due to evolutionary pressure to handle changing environments.
scope: 35 BioModels pathway models versus random gene-circuit models
measurable_quantities: memory capacity after successive random edge rewirings
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Oscillatory pathway networks may gain more memory from noise
claim: Biswas, Clawson and Levin hypothesize that biological networks with strong oscillatory components (such as cell-cycle, circadian-clock and developmental-timer models) may benefit more from noise in terms of memory, analogous to harmonic resonance, though some oscillatory models did not show this.
quote: From this, we hypothesize that biological networks with strong oscillatory components may benefit more, from a memory perspective, to noise, similar to the case of harmonic resonance [122].
scope: ODE models of oscillatory biological networks (cell cycle, circadian clocks, developmental timers)
measurable_quantities: oscillation amplitude
change in memory capacity with noise
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models of circadian and cell-cycle oscillators.

label: Habituation (pharmacoresistance) occurs in every testable pathway model
claim: Modelling pharmacoresistance as habituation (a progressive 50% drop in response across repeated, lengthening stimulations), at least one habituating stimulus–response pair was found in each of the 27 testable BioModels pathway models, with 1–50% of node pairs per model habituating.
quote: Overall, we were able to test 27 out of the 35 models (77%, see Section 4) and at least one instance of habituation was found for each model, with the distribution of pharmacoresistance across all potential models ranging between 1–50% (see Figure 8 and Figures S11–S13).
scope: 27 ODE pathway models from BioModels
measurable_quantities: fraction of UCS–R pairs showing habituation
response-node expression across repeated stimulations
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models; published drug-tolerance time-course data.

label: Pharmacoresistance may be an evolved form of network adaptation
claim: Because random ODE networks rarely show habituation in more than 30% of stimulus–response pairs while biological pathway models differ from that distribution, pharmacoresistance (habituation) may be a form of network adaptation more prevalent in networks shaped by evolutionary pressure, not due to network properties alone.
quote: This would hint that pharmacoresistance may be a form of network adaptation, which would indeed be more prevalent in a biological network shaped by evolutionary pressure.
scope: BioModels pathway models versus 500 random gene-circuit models
measurable_quantities: distribution of habituation prevalence in biological versus random networks
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Stimulating other nodes can break pharmacoresistance in many pathway models
claim: In 17 of the 27 habituating BioModels pathway models (about 63%), stimulating a third node (neither the stimulus nor the response) abolished habituation for some stimulus–response pairs, so some biological networks contain discoverable stimulus nodes that may serve to break pharmacoresistance without rewiring the network.
quote: Overall, we conclude that in some biological networks, there are discoverable stimulus nodes that may serve towards breaking pharmacoresistance.
scope: 27 habituating ODE pathway models from BioModels
measurable_quantities: fraction of UCS–R pairs whose habituation is broken by a third-node stimulus
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models; drug-combination response data such as published drug-synergy screens.

label: Sensitization is common in biological pathway models but rare in random networks
claim: Sensitization (a progressive 1.5-fold increase in response over repeated stimulations) was found in 27 of the 35 BioModels pathway models, whereas very few random gene-circuit models showed it (under 10% of pairings per model), suggesting the feature may be unique to biology or require more complex random models.
quote: Interestingly, very few of the random models had UCS-R relations that generated sensitization (<10% of UCS-R pairings per model), indicating that this feature may be unique to biology, or that more complex random models would be needed to find such behavior (Figure 10 and Figures S17–S19).
scope: 35 BioModels pathway models versus 500 random gene-circuit models
measurable_quantities: fraction of UCS–R pairs showing sensitization
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Sensitization is harder to break than habituation in pathway models
claim: In ODE pathway models, sensitization could be broken by stimulating a third node in only 8 of 27 sensitizing models, mostly for fewer than 5% of node pairs, so breaking sensitization is less likely than breaking habituation and therapies may need other avenues of intervention.
quote: Overall, we conclude that while sensitization is prevalent in biological models, the breaking of sensitization is less likely than in habituation, and therefore therapeutic models may need to pursue other avenues of intervention.
scope: 27 sensitizing ODE pathway models from BioModels
measurable_quantities: fraction of UCS–R pairs whose sensitization is broken
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models.

label: Pulsatile signalling may let cells behaviour-shape each other in vivo
claim: Because transcriptional and other signalling mechanisms are pulsatile, cells may apply timed behaviour-shaping stimuli to each other in vivo, exploiting the trainability of their pathways to evolve complex phenotypes, though the role of trainability in evolution and development is unknown.
quote: The role of trainability in evolution and development is as yet unknown, but it is interesting that transcriptional [126] and other [127,128] biological signaling mechanisms are now seen as pulsatile, which affords rich opportunity for cells to apply timed “behavior shaping” stimuli to each other in vivo, as a way of exploiting the multiscale competency of biological material to evolve complex phenotypes [129].
scope: Cells and tissues in vivo
measurable_quantities: pulse frequency of transcription-factor or signalling activity
history-dependent changes in downstream responses
candidate_data: Live-cell single-cell signalling time courses (e.g. NF-κB, p53, ERK reporter imaging datasets) in the Image Data Resource or Gene Expression Omnibus.

label: Behaviour-shaping of pathways could be an alternative to gene therapy
claim: Rational stimulation regimes derived from computational models of pathway memory could control pathway function without genomic editing or network rewiring, so behaviour-shaping of pathway responses stands as a potential biomedical alternative to gene therapy (e.g. to counter drug pharmacoresistance and sensitization).
quote: Rational control of dynamic pathway function using stimuli derived from computational models opens the door to empirical studies of proto-cognitive capacities in unconventional embodiments and suggests numerous possible applications in biomedicine, where behavior shaping of pathway responses stand as a potential alternative to gene therapy.
scope: Gene regulatory and protein pathways in cells and tissues
measurable_quantities: drug response after model-derived stimulation regimes
pathway output before and after training
candidate_data: none known

label: Biological memory preserves salience rather than fidelity
claim: Levin proposes that memory, across scales from cells to societies, is best understood as preserving salience (what matters for the agent's future) rather than fidelity to the details of the original data.
quote: Using examples from developmental biology, evolution, and synthetic bioengineering, in addition to neuroscience, I propose that a perspective on memory as preserving salience, not fidelity, is applicable to many phenomena on scales from cells to societies.
scope: Living systems from cells to societies
candidate_data: none known

label: Adaptive confabulation resolves the persistence paradox for individuals and lineages
claim: Levin argues that the paradox that a changing agent or species ceases to be itself while an unchanging one dies out is resolved by continuous commitment to creative, adaptive confabulation (reinterpretation of memories and information) at levels from molecular to behavioural, in individuals and whole lineages.
quote: Continuous commitment to creative, adaptive confabulation, from the molecular to the behavioral levels, is the answer to the persistence paradox as it applies to individuals and whole lineages.
scope: Individual organisms and evolutionary lineages
candidate_data: none known

label: Memories may be active agents in the sense-making process
claim: Levin speculates that, on a substrate-independent, processual view of life and mind, memories, as patterns in the excitable medium of cognitive systems, could be seen as minimally agential participants that help shape their own reinterpretation, blurring the line between thoughts and thinkers.
quote: I also speculate that a substrate-independent, processual view of life and mind suggests that memories, as patterns in the excitable medium of cognitive systems, could be seen as active agents in the sense-making process.
scope: Cognitive systems in general
candidate_data: none known

label: Reinterpreting non-local memories is a cognitive glue that makes Selves
claim: Levin proposes that mnemonic improvisation, the ability to modify, remap and interpret non-local memories onto new media and contexts, is one of the kinds of cognitive glue that binds parts into a Self at every scale.
quote: Thus, I propose that the ability to modify and interpret non-local memories is one of the kinds of cognitive glue that reifies Selves (at all scales) [23,24,25].
scope: Agents at all scales, from cells to organisms
candidate_data: none known

label: Memories surviving metamorphosis are remapped to stay salient in the new body
claim: In insects whose memories survive metamorphosis (caterpillar to butterfly), recall does not carry over specific caterpillar memories but generalizes and remaps them (e.g. from leaves to food) so that the learned relationship keeps its salience in the new body and environment.
quote: The process of memory and recall not only functionally generalizes (abstracts20) the information (not leaves, but “food”), but most importantly, remaps21 it in a way that the basic relationship learned maintains its salience in a new body and environment.
scope: Holometabolous insects (e.g. Lepidoptera) retaining learned associations through metamorphosis
measurable_quantities: adult response to larval conditioned cue
behavioural output used by adult versus larva for the same association
candidate_data: Published larval-to-adult conditioning studies in moths and Drosophila; no dedicated database known.

label: Engrams act more like prompts decoded by an intelligent receiver than like encodings
claim: From examples such as frogs that seek out an odorant injected into the egg they developed from, Levin argues that engrams behave less like encoded memories and more like prompts, with much of the work (detecting novelty, remapping across scales, contextualizing and generalizing) done by the encoding and decoding process.
quote: The engrams seem less like encoded memories29, and more like a kind of prompt, with a lot of the hard work being carried out through the encoding/decoding process, which adds interpretation, context sensitivity, and generalization (i.e., intelligence) to the process.
scope: Memory transfer phenomena in animals (frog eggs, Aplysia brain-extract transfer)
candidate_data: none known

label: The same bioelectric trigger is reinterpreted by context (monensin: tails vs legs)
claim: Low-information bioelectric triggers are interpreted by competent tissues according to context: the voltage-modifying reagent monensin induces tail regrowth in tadpoles but leg regrowth in froglets, never the reverse, preserving high-level information such as 'build whatever normally goes at this location'.
quote: Here, the same bioelectric stimulus is functionally reinterpreted based on the specific context, preserving salient, high-level information like “build whatever normally goes at this location” (in the case of the appendage regeneration trigger).
scope: Xenopus tadpole tail and froglet hindlimb regeneration
measurable_quantities: regenerated structure identity after monensin treatment by stage and location
membrane potential at the wound
candidate_data: Published Xenopus regeneration experiments; Xenbase expression and anatomy data.

label: Polyploid newts build normal tubules by switching molecular mechanisms
claim: Engineered polyploid newts with much larger cells keep kidney tubule diameter normal by using fewer cells and, with truly enormous cells, a single cell bending around itself, showing that tissues call up different molecular mechanisms (cytoskeletal bending instead of cell–cell communication) to reach the same anatomical goal state.
quote: This requires using a different molecular mechanism (cytoskeletal bending instead of cell–cell communication of tubulogenesis)—calling up different modular subroutines to accomplish their high-level goal state as needed, while circumstances (indeed, their inner components) change unexpectedly34.
scope: Polyploid newt kidney tubules
measurable_quantities: tubule diameter
cells per tubule cross-section
cell size versus ploidy
candidate_data: Classical histology of polyploid newts (Fankhauser); no modern dataset known.

label: Bowtie compression is common in biochemical, bioelectric and mechanical pathways
claim: Levin argues that a bowtie architecture, which compresses data to a generative kernel that must later be re-inflated and reinterpreted, is common at the subcellular scale in biochemical, bioelectrical and biomechanical pathways, as well as in the egg stage of the metazoan life cycle and in learning.
quote: Note that this bowtie architecture—which forces a compression36 of data to a generative kernel that then has to be re-inflated and elaborated—is also a common feature of biochemical, bioelectrical, and biomechanical pathways (Figure 7), that is, at the subcellular scale;
scope: Subcellular signalling pathways and metazoan life cycles
measurable_quantities: number of inputs, core intermediates and outputs in signalling networks
candidate_data: Pathway databases such as Reactome and KEGG for bowtie structure analysis.

label: Anatomical plasticity across species reflects willingness to confabulate in morphospace
claim: Levin proposes that the spectrum from hardwired, mosaic C. elegans through intermediately plastic amphibians and embryonic mammals to extremely plastic planaria reflects a strategic parameter: the willingness to confabulate in anatomical space, i.e. to rely on pattern extraction and completion rather than taking genetic priors too seriously.
quote: What underlying parameter is represented by the spectrum ranging from the hardwired, mosaic C. elegans to the intermediately plastic amphibia and (embryonic) mammals, and to the extreme plasticity of planaria? I propose it is the willingness to confabulate in anatomical space
scope: Metazoans from C. elegans to amphibians, mammals and planaria
measurable_quantities: regenerative capacity
developmental regulative ability after perturbation
candidate_data: Comparative regeneration and embryonic-perturbation literature; no single database known.

label: Planaria resist cancer and ageing despite noisy genomes via pattern completion
claim: In silico simulations show how lineages such as planarian flatworms can become extremely resistant to transgenesis, ageing, cancer and injury despite very noisy genomes because they commit to a strategy that overrides genetic details with large-scale pattern completion.
quote: In silico simulation results [176] show how this kind of process can give rise to remarkable lineages, such as planarian flatworms, which are extremely resistant to transgenesis, aging, cancer, and injury despite40 their incredibly noisy genome because they have fully committed to a strategy that overrides genetic details with large-scale pattern completion [176].
scope: Planarian flatworms (e.g. Schmidtea mediterranea) and in silico evolutionary models
measurable_quantities: somatic mutation load / genome heterogeneity
regeneration fidelity
tumour incidence
lifespan
candidate_data: PlanMine and SmedGD planarian genome and transcriptome resources; comparative regeneration data.

label: Substrate unreliability is the reason, not an obstacle, for biological intelligence
claim: Levin argues that the noise and unreliability of biological matter is a feature rather than a bug: morphological and behavioural intelligence arose because of, not in spite of, the vulnerability of the substrate, as suggested by planaria having the noisiest genome and the best regeneration and cancer resistance.
quote: It seems that the underlying noise and unreliability of biological matter is not a bug but a feature: we obtained morphological (and behavioral) intelligence because of, not in spite of, the vulnerability of the substrate45.
scope: Living organisms, especially metazoans
measurable_quantities: genomic noise
regenerative and morphogenetic competency across species
candidate_data: Comparative genomics (e.g. Ensembl) and regeneration literature; no direct dataset known.

label: Cellular competency hides genome quality from selection, driving an intelligence ratchet
claim: Because competent biological material compensates for defects, selection cannot see genome quality clearly, so more evolutionary change accrues in competency mechanisms than in structural components, producing a positive-feedback intelligence ratchet based on remapping information to new contexts.
quote: The competency of our material means that selection cannot see the quality of genomes clearly46. More evolutionary work thus has to be conducted on the competency mechanisms, not the structural components, leading to a positive feedback loop—an intelligence ratchet based on the remapping of information to new contexts47.
scope: Evolution of multicellular organisms; in silico evolutionary models
measurable_quantities: rate of evolution of competency versus structural genes
fitness masking by developmental compensation
candidate_data: Comparative genomic rate data (e.g. Ensembl Compara); in silico evolution simulations.

label: There is no single substrate for memory; all components can serve as scratchpads
claim: Levin hypothesizes that there is no single substrate for memory: every component of a living system can use everything in its environment, including the high-dimensional reservoir of subcellular structure, as an interpretable scratchpad, rather than engrams residing only in synapses.
quote: My current hypothesis, driven by the above multi-scale perspective [218], is that there is no single substrate for memory49.
scope: Nervous systems and non-neural tissues
measurable_quantities: memory retention after disruption of synaptic versus non-synaptic substrates
candidate_data: Published memory-transfer and post-amputation memory experiments (e.g. Aplysia RNA transfer, planarian memory retention); no database known.

label: Training associative memories may increase integration of composite systems
claim: Levin proposes that memories belonging to a collective (e.g. a rat's lever–reward association, which no single cell experiences) may help reify the collective Self, and that training associative memories into gene regulatory networks should be tested for increases in integrated information (self-coherence).
quote: This is currently being investigated in the context of our training of associative memories into gene-regulatory networks and other substrates, with measures of integrated information to determine if the forming of memories increases the self-coherence of composite systems.
scope: Gene regulatory network models and other composite systems
measurable_quantities: integrated information (Φ or related measures) before and after associative training
candidate_data: BioModels curated ODE models for in silico training.

label: Behavioural intelligence evolved from morphogenetic problem-solving
claim: Levin proposes that behavioural intelligence in 3D space evolved from morphogenetic problem-solving competencies in anatomical space, which were themselves required by the inevitability of mutation and injury.
quote: Behavioral intelligence in 3D space evolved from morphogenetic problem-solving competencies in anatomical space [97,124].
scope: Evolution of animals with nervous systems
measurable_quantities: phylogenetic origin of ion channels, gap junctions and neurotransmitters in non-neural developmental roles
candidate_data: Comparative genomics of ion-channel and gap-junction families (e.g. Ensembl Compara, Pfam).

label: Consciousness may be palpated uncertainty about one's own memories
claim: Extending Solms's idea that consciousness is palpated uncertainty about the outside world, Levin hypothesizes that consciousness is palpated uncertainty about one's own memories and internal states.
quote: I propose to expand this idea, with the hypothesis that consciousness is palpated uncertainty about your own memories and internal states.
scope: Conscious agents
candidate_data: none known

label: Self-assembly emerges from cells sharing a common model of organismal form
claim: In simulations based on variational free-energy minimization (active inference), cells that share a common genetically and epigenetically specified model of the organism's form self-assemble into that form, offering a proof of principle that self-assembly can be an emergent property of such cells.
quote: Here, we offer a proof of principle that self-assembly is an emergent property of cells that share a common (genetic and epigenetic) model of organismal form.
scope: Active-inference simulation of eight cells forming a head–body–tail morphology
measurable_quantities: final cell positions and identities versus target morphology
ensemble free energy over time
candidate_data: SPM software (spm_ADEM.m) for reproducing the simulation; none known for empirical data.

label: Genome parametrizes a generative model; epigenesis inverts it
claim: Under the free-energy account of morphogenesis, genetic codes can be interpreted as parametrizing a generative model that predicts the signals each cell would sense in the target morphology, and epigenetic processes (signalling-dependent transcription) as the inversion of that model.
quote: This novel perspective on the coordination of migration and differentiation of cells suggests an interpretation of genetic codes as parametrizing a generative model—predicting the signals sensed by cells in the target morphology—and epigenetic processes as the subsequent inversion of that model.
scope: Morphogenesis in multicellular organisms
candidate_data: none known

label: Morphogenesis requires each cell to model its place in the target form
claim: Friston, Levin, Sengupta and Pezzulo propose that morphogenetic self-organization requires each cell to have an implicit model of its place in the final morphology, with self-assembly being cells moving to sample the local signals that model predicts (minimizing variational free energy).
quote: In this paper, we pursue the notion that morphogenetic self-organization requires each cell to have an implicit model of its place in the final morphology [21]—and that self-assembly is the process of moving to sample local signals that are predicted by that model.
scope: Cells during embryogenesis and regeneration
measurable_quantities: cell migration trajectories relative to signal gradients
signal concentrations sensed at final positions
candidate_data: Live-imaging cell-tracking datasets of embryogenesis (e.g. in the Image Data Resource or Cell Tracking Challenge).

label: Free energy is minimized only when every cell occupies a unique inferred place
claim: In the active-inference model of morphogenesis, where identical pluripotent cells share one generative model, the minimum of variational free energy is reached only when every cell is at a unique location and has correctly inferred its place, so free-energy minimization guarantees convergence to the target form.
quote: This is guaranteed because the minimum of variational free energy is obtained when each cell is in a unique location and has correctly inferred its place.
scope: Active-inference model of morphogenesis with cells sharing a generative model
measurable_quantities: ensemble free energy
uniqueness of cell identity assignments
candidate_data: none known

label: Simulated cells resolve fate ambiguity using context set by other ambiguous cells
claim: In the active-inference simulation, identical undifferentiated cells starting at one location migrate rapidly to their target locations and then differentiate (around the eighth time step) into head, body and tail types as ensemble free energy falls, showing cells can resolve ambiguity about their fate even when it depends on context set by other equally ambiguous cells.
quote: These results are compelling in the sense that they show cells can resolve ambiguity about their fate, even when that resolution depends upon the context established by other (equally ambiguous) cells.
scope: Active-inference simulation of eight cells forming a head–body–tail morphology
measurable_quantities: cell identity confusion matrix over time
time to migration and differentiation
candidate_data: SPM software (spm_ADEM.m) for reproducing the simulation.

label: Bisected simulated embryos regenerate the full target form
claim: When the partially differentiated simulated embryo is cut in two and each half's cells are replicated, the cells undergo slight dedifferentiation and then each half regenerates the complete head–body–tail target morphology, illustrating pluripotency and recovery from drastic interventions in the active-inference model.
quote: This example illustrates the pluripotential nature of the cells and the ability of self-assembly to recover from fairly drastic interventions.
scope: Active-inference morphogenesis simulation (analogous to planarian or regulative embryo bisection)
measurable_quantities: morphology of each half after continued simulation
degree of dedifferentiation
candidate_data: SPM software for the simulation; planarian regeneration data (e.g. PlanMine) for comparison.

label: Altering signal sensitivity without changing the model predicts specific birth defects
claim: In the active-inference morphogenesis model, changing cells' sensitivity to extracellular, exogenous or intracellular signals without changing the generative model produces specific dysmorphogenesis, e.g. reducing sensitivity to the head-expressed signal shrinks the head, and doubling sensitivity to intracellular signals causes failed migration, differentiation and atrophy; these are predictions for pharmacological manipulation of intercellular signalling.
quote: More selective interventions produce a dysmorphogenesis of various segments of the target morphology: reducing sensitivity to the second chemotactic signal—that is expressed by head cells—reduces the size of the head.
scope: Active-inference morphogenesis simulation; proposed for real embryos under signalling perturbation
measurable_quantities: size of body segments after altered signal-receptor sensitivity
differentiation of cell types
candidate_data: Teratogen and receptor-inhibitor phenotype data in model-organism databases such as ZFIN and Xenbase.

label: An exogenous gradient makes self-assembly more robust for larger ensembles
claim: In the active-inference morphogenesis simulations, an exogenous concentration gradient is not necessary but yields a more robust solution for larger ensembles (more than four clones) and fixes the orientation of the target morphology relative to an external frame of reference.
quote: This is not a necessary component of the scheme; however, our simulations suggest that it underwrites a more robust solution for larger ensembles (with more than four clones).
scope: Active-inference morphogenesis simulation
measurable_quantities: accuracy of final morphology with and without exogenous gradient as ensemble size varies
candidate_data: SPM software (spm_ADEM.m) for reproducing the simulation.

label: Epigenetic active inference is indispensable for patterning beyond genetic encoding
claim: Although aspects of the target morphology are genetically encoded in the parameters of cells' generative models, epigenetic processes (active inference) are indispensable for patterning, consistent with the regenerative target morphology of planaria being permanently alterable (to two heads) by a brief modification of electric synapses.
quote: It may be worth concluding that although aspects of the target morphology are genetically encoded (in the parameters of the generative models); epigenetic processes (active inference) are indispensable for patterning.
scope: Morphogenesis and regeneration, e.g. planarian regeneration
measurable_quantities: persistence of altered target morphology without genetic change
candidate_data: Published planarian gap-junction-blockade regeneration data; PlanMine.

label: Neural and bioelectric patterning networks may share dynamics
claim: Because non-neuronal cells use many of the same ion-channel and electrical-synapse mechanisms as neurons for pattern formation and repair, significant commonalities may exist between the dynamics of neural networks and of bioelectric signalling networks that control shape, so neural modelling tools such as dynamic causal modelling may apply to morphogenesis data.
quote: This suggests the possibility that significant commonalities may exist between the dynamics of neural networks and of bioelectric signalling networks that control shape determination [20,21,83].
scope: Non-neural tissues with bioelectric signalling during development and regeneration
measurable_quantities: ion-channel and gap-junction expression in non-neural patterning tissues
fit of dynamic causal models to bioelectric time-series
candidate_data: Ion-channel expression in developing tissues (Xenbase, Gene Expression Omnibus); voltage-dye imaging data in the Image Data Resource where available.
